passage:
Rain hammered the tin roof of the school shed as the carrom final ended. Amandeep had led until the last two coins, then missed both, and the room filled with applause for the other side. Water dripped through a leak onto his sleeve. He stared at the board, sure everyone was thinking he had thrown it away.
The shed emptied fast, everybody racing the storm. Jatin didn't. He dropped onto the wet bench beside Amandeep.
"I still respect you," Jatin said. "That last shot was brutal luck."
Amandeep's shoulders loosened. He couldn't speak, so he nodded. "Thanks," he managed at last. "When it's your turn to lose, I'm sitting right here."

qa.q: What was the final game that Amandeep lost?
qa.a: It was a carrom final.

qa.q: What was Amandeep feeling as the room applauded the other side, and what did he feel after Jatin sat down?
qa.a: He felt ashamed and sure everyone thought he had thrown it away, and then relief as his shoulders loosened when Jatin stayed.

qa.q: How can Amandeep respond to Jatin's kindness?
qa.a: He can accept the comfort now and, as he promised, sit beside Jatin when Jatin loses. 🙂

qa.q: How might Jatin see Amandeep's missed shot?
qa.a: He sees it as brutal luck, not a reason to stop respecting a friend, so he stays while everyone else runs from the storm.

grounding: A friend says he still respects Amandeep and sits with him after a public loss, and Amandeep feels relief and plans to return the kindness.

passage:
Kishore crossed the line fourth at the district sprint trials and bent over, hands on his knees, listening to his own lungs. When he looked up, Coach Gurleen was at the fence with her arms folded and a frown he had never seen on her. He wished the track would swallow him. On the auto ride home he pictured her deciding he wasn't worth the extra sessions.
Next morning he went to the ground early. "Ma'am," he said, his voice shaky, "what should I fix first?"
The frown eased into something tired and honest. "I was frowning at the clock, not at you," she said. "Your first twenty metres. Come, let's film it."

qa.q: Where did Kishore finish at the district sprint trials?
qa.a: He finished fourth.

qa.q: What did Kishore fear the coach's frown meant?
qa.a: He feared she had decided he wasn't worth the extra sessions.

qa.q: Which choice worked for Kishore, and why?
qa.a: Going back early and asking what to fix worked, because it turned a frown into useful information instead of a verdict.

qa.q: What might Coach Gurleen have been feeling at the fence?
qa.a: She may have been tired and frustrated at the time on the clock, and not rejecting Kishore, since she offered to film his start.

grounding: A coach's frown after a poor result feels like rejection to the teen, who asks what he can learn instead of assuming total disapproval.

passage:
I'm Mridul, and I share a hostel room with Eshaan. He failed the inter-house coding contest in the dining hall when his screen froze on the projector. Everybody clapped politely. He said "no problem" and went to bed at eight, which is not like him.
The next morning there was a sticky note on his desk: "Thirty minutes a day. One small program." It was nothing like the giant project he'd been describing all term. Every evening after that he did it, with the door open, humming.
I can't say whether he still felt bad underneath. Maybe he did. But last week he told me most well-known programmers fail loudly once and keep going quietly. Then he asked me to test his little program.

qa.q: What was written on the sticky note on Eshaan's desk?
qa.a: It said "Thirty minutes a day. One small program."

qa.q: What might Eshaan have been feeling on the night of the contest?
qa.a: He may have felt embarrassed or low: he said 'no problem' but went to bed at eight, which is not like him, though Mridul can't be sure.

qa.q: What worked in Eshaan's way of restarting?
qa.a: He replaced the giant project with a small daily step and asked a friend to test his work, so progress came from practice and correction.

qa.q: How does Mridul see Eshaan's recovery?
qa.a: Mridul sees it cautiously: he can't be sure how Eshaan feels inside, but he notices the routine, the humming and the request to test the program.

grounding: After failing, a teen restarts with a smaller plan; an observer sees the daily practice and the remark that people fail often, quietly.

passage:
At the Cape Town schools' swimming gala, Siddiq touched the wall a full second slower than the qualifying time he needed. He hung on the lane rope, chest heaving, watching the board.
Thabo, who had beaten him last term, leaned over from the next lane. "Was that your best? Maybe the regional team isn't for you." A couple of his friends laughed.
Siddiq felt his jaw clench. He wanted to fire back. Instead he pulled himself out, dried his face and said, "Well swum." Thabo blinked and walked off.
That evening Siddiq wrote his time on the kitchen whiteboard, next to his best from last month. "Beat this one," he wrote underneath. His father added a smiley.

qa.q: What did Thabo say to Siddiq at the gala?
qa.a: He said, "Was that your best? Maybe the regional team isn't for you."

qa.q: What did Siddiq want to do when Thabo gloated, and why might he have held back?
qa.a: He wanted to fire back, since his jaw clenched, but he chose to say 'Well swum' and to put his effort into his own time instead.

qa.q: What was wise about writing his time on the whiteboard?
qa.a: It turned his attention from the rival to his own past score, giving him something he could actually work on.

qa.q: What might Thabo have been feeling when he leaned over the lane rope?
qa.a: Thabo may have been keen to stay ahead, since he had beaten Siddiq before, and his surprise at 'Well swum' suggests he expected an argument.

grounding: A rival gloats over Siddiq's failure; he doesn't stoop, and aims to beat his own past score.

passage:
At the school activity fair, sign-up tables lined the hall. Dolma read every sheet twice. Poetry slam: what if she forgot the words? Debate: what if she was bad? Art contest: what if hers was the worst? She put her hands in her pockets and walked past all of them.
Anirban, holding a marker at the open-mic table, waved her over. "Try this one. Two minutes, four people, no marks."
"I'd probably mess up."
"Then you'll have messed up in front of four people. Not forty."
Dolma read four lines of a poem, her hands shaking. Nobody clapped loudly, but Anirban nodded, and her stomach unclenched. She took the marker and slowly wrote her name on the sheet for next week.

qa.q: How many people were at the open-mic table?
qa.a: There were four people.

qa.q: Why did Dolma walk past all the sign-up tables?
qa.a: She was afraid of failing: forgetting the words, being bad, being the worst, so she avoided anything she might fail at.

qa.q: What small step helped Dolma start?
qa.a: Trying a low-stakes attempt, two minutes in front of four people with no marks, made failing feel survivable.

qa.q: How does Anirban see Dolma's fear?
qa.a: Anirban sees it as small enough to face, and offers a low-stakes chance without judging her.

grounding: Dolma refuses to try things she might fail at; a low-stakes first attempt shows that fear of failure limits her more than failure would.

passage:
Thursday, 10 pm. I failed the chemistry test. I hid the paper in my bag all afternoon and my stomach hurt through dinner. When Papa asked what was wrong, I burst into tears. I was ready for shouting.
Instead Mummy came round the table and hugged me. Papa started to speak and she said, "Let her breathe first." Then she said, "That must have felt awful." I thought I would feel small, but I felt safe.
So I told them the truth: I skipped revision because I was scared I wouldn't understand it. Mummy and I made a plan for tomorrow evening, one chapter, and I'll explain it back to her. I'll ask Ms. Iqbal to go through the test with me.
Vasudha

qa.q: Which test did Vasudha fail?
qa.a: She failed the chemistry test.

qa.q: What did Vasudha expect when she burst into tears, and what did she feel instead?
qa.a: She expected shouting, but she felt safe when Mummy hugged her and said it must have felt awful.

qa.q: What next step did Vasudha and her mother plan?
qa.a: They planned one chapter for tomorrow evening that Vasudha will explain back, and Vasudha will ask Ms. Iqbal to go through the test.

qa.q: What might Mummy have understood about Vasudha's tears?
qa.a: Mummy may have understood that Vasudha was already hurting and scared, so she put comfort first and asked Papa to let Vasudha breathe.

grounding: A parent comforts the teen instead of scolding after a failure, she feels safe, and shares honestly so that they plan the next step together.

passage:
Counsellor's note, Monday. Indu asked to see me privately. She had seen her close friend Payal send unkind messages about a new girl to a group chat. Indu felt torn: Payal is her friend, and she did not want to be the one who told. That afternoon, on the way to the bus, she spoke to Payal first. Payal called it a joke.
On Thursday Indu came back. The messages had continued and the new girl had stopped coming to lunch. Indu said, "Being loyal to Payal can't mean staying quiet about this." She gave me the dates and what she had seen.
I thanked her, then spoke with the new girl's family and with Payal separately, without naming Indu. I will follow up with both girls next week.
Mr. Bose

qa.q: Where did Indu speak to Payal?
qa.a: She spoke to Payal on the way to the bus.

qa.q: Why did Indu feel torn?
qa.a: Payal is her friend and she did not want to be the one who told, yet the messages were hurting the new girl.

qa.q: What order of steps worked for Indu, and what could she do if things continue?
qa.a: She talked to Payal first and, when the harm continued, told a trusted adult with dates; she could keep checking on the new girl.

qa.q: How might the new girl have experienced the messages?
qa.a: She stopped coming to lunch, which suggests she felt hurt and wanted to avoid other students.

grounding: A teen torn between loyalty and right talks to the friend first, then tells a trusted adult when the bullying continues.

passage:
I'm Gautam, and I sit two benches from Jaya. Last week she told the principal that some senior boys were taking a first-year's lunch money. Since then her old group calls her "snitch." Yesterday they walked off when she sat down, and one of them said loudly, "Some people can't keep their mouths shut."
She ate lunch on the steps. I joined her, though I didn't know what to say. She mentioned she had told only to keep the first-year safe, not to get anybody punished. Her eyes were red, but she also said she would do it again.
I can't tell how much it hurts underneath. Two girls from our class waved at her today. Maybe that's a start.

qa.q: What does Jaya's old group call her?
qa.a: They call her "snitch."

qa.q: What might Jaya be feeling underneath, according to Gautam?
qa.a: She may be hurt and lonely, since her eyes were red, yet also sure she was right, because she says she would do it again; Gautam admits he can't tell.

qa.q: How could Jaya cope with being frozen out?
qa.a: She can hold on to the difference between telling to protect and telling to punish, and lean on allies like Gautam and the two girls who waved.

qa.q: How might Jaya's old group see what she did?
qa.a: They see it as betraying the group, which is why they call it snitching, while Jaya sees it as keeping the first-year safe.

grounding: After reporting a wrong, a teen is called a snitch and frozen out by her group; an observer sees the hurt and the beginnings of new allies.

Monday. Keerthana noticed that whenever Sahil opened the class group chat, his shoulders dropped. Over his shoulder she saw messages calling him names. Her first thought was to shout at the boys at recess. She wrote down the dates instead.
Wednesday. She waited outside Mr. Ghosh's room, the teacher she trusted most. "I'd like to tell you something, but please don't say it came from me. It's about Sahil." She gave him the dates and what she had seen, with no guesses. He thanked her and said he would handle it carefully.
The next Tuesday she asked, "Sir, is Sahil okay?" Mr. Ghosh nodded. "It's being dealt with. You did the right thing." The messages had stopped, and Sahil sat beside her at lunch.

qa.q: On which day did Keerthana speak to Mr. Ghosh?
qa.a: She spoke to him on Wednesday.

qa.q: What might Keerthana have been feeling as she waited outside Mr. Ghosh's room?
qa.a: She was probably nervous but determined, since she asked that it not be said the news came from her.

qa.q: What made Keerthana's report useful, and what did she do afterwards?
qa.a: She gave dates and what she had seen with no guesses, and she followed up the next Tuesday instead of taking matters into her own hands.

qa.q: How might Sahil have experienced the change by the following week?
qa.a: Sahil probably felt relief when the messages stopped, and sitting beside Keerthana at lunch suggests he felt supported.

grounding: A teen reports harassment of a classmate to a trusted teacher with facts, asks for confidentiality and follows up, over three days.

passage:
I'm Keerthana, and honestly this one still makes me angry. I told our class teacher that boys were sending cruel messages about a girl in my grade. I gave dates. For two weeks, nothing happened. Then in assembly the teacher said, "Some people have been complaining, and we know who." Everybody turned to look at me. I felt betrayed, like I'd been thrown to the wolves.
That night I told my cousin Sahil. He said, "Don't stop. Write it all down and go higher." So I emailed the principal with the dates, my parents came with me to meet the principal, and we found out about the board's helpline. I stayed with my friends at lunch and didn't go anywhere alone until it was sorted.
It took time, but in the end it was taken seriously.

qa.q: How long did Keerthana wait with nothing happening?
qa.a: She waited for two weeks.

qa.q: How did Keerthana feel when the class teacher spoke in assembly?
qa.a: She felt betrayed, like she'd been thrown to the wolves, as everybody turned to look at her.

qa.q: What steps could someone take if a school ignores or exposes a report?
qa.a: They can keep written dates, email the principal, bring parents, use the board's helpline and stay with friends until it is sorted.

qa.q: How does Sahil see what Keerthana should do?
qa.a: Sahil tells her not to stop, and sees writing everything down and going higher as the way to be taken seriously.

grounding: A teen's report is ignored and then exposed, she feels betrayed, documents, escalates to the principal and helpline, and keeps herself safe.
